analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal bureau that reviews and caps brand-name drug prices, with rebates to patients when prices are too high.
analysis.headline: A bill by Sen. Booker to set up a federal drug-price regulator was referred to the Senate health committee in July 2024 and died there without a hearing, vote, or action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new government bureau to review the prices of expensive prescription drugs. Drug makers would have to disclose their costs, research spending, profits, patents, and foreign prices. For many brand-name drugs, the bureau would set a maximum price based on the median price charged in 11 other wealthy countries, and companies charging too much would have to cut prices, pay back excess revenue to patients, or lose the exclusive rights protecting their drug from cheaper copies.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients paying high prices for brand-name drugs, especially those with little or no insurance coverage, along with Medicare and Medicaid, which would pay less for drugs found to be overpriced. Patients could petition the bureau directly and would receive rebates when a price was ruled too high.

how_it_helps.text: For most brand-name drugs without generic competition, the bureau would set an interim maximum price equal to the lower of the median price in 11 reference countries or a bureau-determined appropriate price.

If a manufacturer failed to lower a price found inappropriate, the Secretary could authorize other entities to use the drug's patents and exclusivities to make a cheaper version, and the bill expressly allows government-run drug manufacturing.
Manufacturers would have to remit excess revenue earned from an inappropriate price, with the money distributed to patients who were overcharged.
Price increases faster than inflation would be presumed inappropriate unless the manufacturer justified them, and any drug with $5 billion in global revenue would face a mandatory price review.

Patients could petition the bureau about drug prices, and a Consumer Advisory Council made up mostly of patients would advise it; the bill would also repeal Medicare's 'non-interference' clause, the rule that has barred Medicare from negotiating drug prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices, profits, and patent leverage would be capped and clawed back, plus taxpayers funding the new bureau at $50 million per year. Some reduction in industry investment in new drugs is the cost supporters would have to acknowledge.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory price caps and government-authorized generic competition could reduce pharmaceutical companies' expected returns, which critics argue would slow investment in developing new medicines over time.

Using patent overrides to enforce prices is a novel and legally untested power, and the bill likely would have faced court challenges and required substantial new federal machinery, funded at $50 million a year.

The interim price formula relies on list prices in foreign countries, which can mask the large rebates drug makers pay in the U.S. system, so the benchmark could be imperfect even in the bill's own terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who take expensive brand-name drugs, the upside is potentially large: real price ceilings, rebates, and a complaint process. The costs fall mainly on one highly profitable industry, though the honest tradeoff is the risk of some slowdown in new drug development, and the bill's heavy reliance on untested patent-override enforcement made its design aggressive rather than cautious.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability and Access Act in the Senate on July 30, 2024, 'for himself and Mr. Sanders.'
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; the action history records no further action of any kind.
It attracted a single cosponsor, an Independent senator, in addition to the sponsor.

The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still sitting in committee, so none of its provisions — the price bureau, the foreign-price benchmarks, the patient rebates, or the repeal of Medicare's non-interference clause — ever took effect or received a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they face no new federal price regulator, no inflation-based price caps, and no risk of losing patent exclusivity, while patients continue to pay U.S. prices that often run well above those in other wealthy countries.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only additional supporter.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote, per the complete action history.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and floor leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote; with no committee action, it had no path forward.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators supported the bill — one Democrat and one Independent — and no senator voted against it because it never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cap their prices at foreign-country medians, force disclosure of costs and profits, claw back excess revenue, and revoke patent exclusivity from companies that refuse to cut prices. Their gain under the status quo is the higher prices patients pay.

The bill would require manufacturers to report the net prices after rebates paid to and from PBMs, shining light on the middleman rebate chain. It imposes no direct price controls on PBMs, so the effect on them is mainly transparency.
If the government authorized use of a brand drug's patents for refusing to cut prices, generic makers could manufacture cheaper versions at a government-set fair compensation.
